issues.subcategory: Contradictory SESOI values
issues.description: The manuscript states two contradictory values for the SESOI used to define the equivalence region. First, it states δ = .27, then later in the same section derives and states the SESOI as δ = |.11|. These cannot both be correct. The δ = .27 value appears to have been inadvertently carried over from the β = .270 effect reported for Study 1, Sample 3 of Grubbs, Kraus, et al. (2020), which is used later as a fallback equivalence boundary. This contradiction fundamentally undermines the pre-registered equivalence testing plan, as the choice of SESOI determines whether null hypotheses for gambling and substance use are supported or rejected.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27. ... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11 ... Collectively, then, setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11| represents an extremely conservative analytic decision.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent Cohen's d values for the same effect
issues.description: For the same study and the same effect (Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020; ΔR² = .012, f² = .016), two different Cohen's d values are reported: d = .22 in the first enumeration and d = .25 in a later sentence. These refer to the same finding from the same source and cannot both be correct.
issues.quote: ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020 ... β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020

issues.subcategory: PGSI response scale mismatch between methods and supplemental materials
issues.description: The methods section describes the PGSI as using a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always), which matches the standard PGSI scoring. However, the supplemental materials show the PGSI response options coded as Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), Almost Always (5). These values are non-standard and inconsistent with the methods description. This discrepancy would produce fundamentally different scores and would invalidate use of published norms and cut-offs for the PGSI.
issues.quote: on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged. [Methods] ... Never (0) Sometimes (2) Most of the time (4) Almost Always (5) [Supplemental]

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale mismatch between methods and supplemental materials
issues.description: The methods section describes the Brief Pornography Screen as using a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often) with responses summed. However, the supplemental materials show response options coded as Never (0), Occasionally (2), Very Often (4). If the supplemental materials reflect the actual survey implementation, scores would range from 0–20 rather than 0–10, invalidating published validation data and clinical cut-offs.
issues.quote: on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed. [Methods] ... Never (0) Occasionally (2) Very Often (4) [Supplemental]

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent definition of moral incongruence operationalization
issues.description: In one passage, the manuscript describes the key operationalization as 'the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action,' but throughout the rest of the manuscript, moral incongruence is consistently defined as the interaction of moral disapproval with frequency of a behavior. These are conceptually and empirically distinct operationalizations.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: Non-comparable outcome measures across behaviors
issues.description: Pornography and gambling are assessed with validated, behavior-specific instruments (BPS and PGSI) while all substances are assessed only with modified NIDA-ASSIST items. This measurement asymmetry means any difference in moral incongruence effects between pornography/gambling and substances could be attributable to measurement sensitivity differences rather than true substantive differences. The central hypothesis (that moral incongruence is unique to pornography) cannot be cleanly tested when the outcome measures are not psychometrically comparable.
issues.quote: Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items ... Alcohol | Average of modified NIDA-ASSIST items for specific substances

issues.subcategory: Averaging items on incompatible response scales
issues.description: The NIDA-ASSIST problematic use composite averages three frequency items scored 0–5 with two items scored on a 0/3/6 scale. Averaging these items without standardization gives the 0/3/6 items disproportionate weight in the composite. This creates a measure whose psychometric properties are unknown and potentially problematic, as items with larger numerical ranges dominate the average.
issues.quote: Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: Unvalidated extension of NIDA-ASSIST to pornography and gambling
issues.description: The NIDA-ASSIST was developed and validated for substance use screening. Extending it to pornography and gambling without validation studies means the psychometric properties (reliability, validity, sensitivity/specificity) are unknown for these behaviors. While the authors acknowledge this, they use these modified ASSIST items as the basis for one of the two pornography analyses and as the gambling parallel measure, making it central to the hypothesis tests.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: Sports-wagering oversample confounds gambling analyses
issues.description: The combined sample includes 1,500 participants specifically recruited for having a past-year history of sports wagering, combined with 2,500 nationally representative participants. For gambling analyses, this creates a sample that is not nationally representative and likely has a very different distribution of gambling frequency, moral attitudes toward gambling, and gambling problems compared to the general population. The effective N of 3,325 gamblers includes this oversample, but no weighting strategy or separate analysis plan is described to account for this design feature. This could substantially bias estimates of moral incongruence effects for gambling.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: No correction for multiple comparisons across primary hypothesis tests
issues.description: Eight moderation analyses are planned as primary hypothesis tests, but no correction for multiple testing is specified for these focal analyses. While Holm-adjusted statistics are mentioned for bivariate correlations, the primary moderation analyses that directly test the hypotheses have no multiplicity adjustment. With 8 tests at α = .05, the family-wise error rate is inflated, which is especially concerning for a registered report aiming to demonstrate that only 1 of 8 interactions is significant.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: Questionable effect size conversions across metrics
issues.description: The manuscript converts between ΔR², f², Cohen's d, and β for interaction effects in multiple regression. However, direct conversion between d and f² assumes a two-group balanced design, which does not apply to continuous interaction effects in regression. For example, ΔR² = .014 with f² = .020 yields d = .24 by the authors' calculation, but d = 2√(.020) ≈ .283 using the standard formula. These conversions across metrics are inappropriate for regression interaction terms and may lead to incorrect power calculations or SESOI specifications.
issues.quote: ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020

issues.subcategory: Power analysis conducted for NHST rather than equivalence testing
issues.description: The power analyses in Table 2 appear to be standard power analyses for detecting effects (NHST), not power analyses for equivalence tests. Equivalence testing generally requires larger samples to achieve adequate power than NHST for the same effect size, because the goal is to reject that the true effect exceeds the bounds rather than to reject a nil null. The achieved power estimates for substances may be substantially overestimated for the equivalence testing context.
issues.quote: we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest (f2 = .015)

issues.subcategory: Directional causal language with cross-sectional design
issues.description: Despite acknowledging the cross-sectional nature of the data as a limitation, the hypotheses and framing consistently use directional/causal language (e.g., 'predict,' 'affects,' 'contributes to'). Cross-sectional moderation analyses cannot establish temporal ordering or causation. Self-perceived addiction could drive moral disapproval rather than the reverse, or both could be driven by an unmeasured third variable.
issues.quote: moral incongruence regarding pornography use will predict self-reported feelings of addiction ... moral disapproval of pornography on self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be significant and positive

issues.subcategory: Underspecified handling of regression assumption violations
issues.description: The plan states that if regression assumptions are 'substantially violated,' supplemental analyses will be conducted, but does not specify what threshold constitutes a 'substantial' violation, which specific alternative methods would be used, or how decisions between OLS and alternatives would be documented. This leaves considerable undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: Fallback equivalence region creates post-hoc hypothesis
issues.description: If the primary SESOI-based equivalence test fails, the authors propose redefining the equivalence region using the lower bound of the 95% CI from their pornography analysis. This means the equivalence region for the fallback analysis is determined by the data itself, introducing circularity and analytic flexibility. The hypothesis changes from 'the effect is practically null' to 'the effect is smaller than the pornography effect,' which is a substantively different and weaker claim.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: No contingency plan for missing data
issues.description: The manuscript states that no unplanned missingness is anticipated due to YouGov's quality controls, but provides no plan for handling missing data should it occur. This is overly optimistic; even well-managed online panels can produce item-level missingness, particularly on sensitive topics like pornography use, substance use, and moral attitudes. Without a pre-specified plan (e.g., listwise deletion, multiple imputation), missing data handling becomes another researcher degree of freedom.
issues.quote: we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: Single-item moral disapproval measure
issues.description: Moral disapproval for each behavior is measured with a single item ('I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'). Single items cannot capture the multidimensional nature of moral judgments, have unknown reliability, and are susceptible to response biases. Furthermore, moral disapproval of a substance one uses may reflect guilt, stigma awareness, or social desirability rather than genuine moral beliefs, and a single item cannot disentangle these. Given that moral disapproval is a central construct, this measurement limitation could substantially affect the validity of all findings.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement "I believe that using ________ is morally wrong" on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: Moral disapproval conflated with guilt in BPS
issues.description: Item 5 of the Brief Pornography Screen ('You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it') directly measures guilt-related continued use, which overlaps conceptually with moral incongruence/moral disapproval. This creates artificial criterion contamination: the predictor (moral disapproval) and a component of the outcome measure (guilt about use) share construct variance, potentially inflating the observed relationship between moral incongruence and BPS scores for pornography relative to outcomes for other behaviors that lack this built-in overlap.
issues.quote: 5. You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.

issues.subcategory: Asymmetric moral disapproval distributions across behaviors
issues.description: The base rates of moral disapproval likely differ dramatically across the target behaviors (e.g., moral disapproval of illicit drug use is likely near-universal, while moral disapproval of alcohol is likely rare). These distributional differences mean that the interaction of moral disapproval × frequency will have very different statistical properties across behaviors—with restricted range in moral disapproval for some behaviors severely limiting the ability to detect interaction effects. Null findings for substances may simply reflect floor/ceiling effects in moral disapproval rather than true absence of moral incongruence effects.
issues.quote: we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement "I believe that using ________ is morally wrong"

issues.subcategory: Confirmatory framing biases study design
issues.description: The stated purpose is 'demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors' and 'with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique.' This confirmatory framing, where the researchers aim to demonstrate rather than test a specific outcome, is inconsistent with the logic of registered reports, which should specify hypotheses to be tested rather than conclusions to be demonstrated. This framing may have influenced design decisions (e.g., the conservative SESOI, use of equivalence testing for non-pornography outcomes) in ways that favor the preferred conclusion.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors

issues.subcategory: Asymmetric hypothesis structure favors desired conclusion
issues.description: The hypotheses are structured asymmetrically: for pornography, the authors use standard NHST (predicting a significant positive effect), while for gambling and substances, they use equivalence testing (predicting null effects). This asymmetry inherently favors the desired conclusion because NHST and equivalence testing have different error structures. Finding significance with NHST is relatively easy with large samples, while failing to reject in equivalence testing with underpowered samples is also common. A more balanced approach would apply the same inferential framework across all behaviors.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral incongruence regarding pornography use will predict self-reported feelings of addiction ... However, we do not expect to find that the interaction of moral disapproval of gambling and gambling frequency will significantly predict self-reported gambling disorder symptoms.

issues.subcategory: Gender operationalization
issues.description: Gender is coded as 'binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male.' This collapses all non-male gender identities into a single reference category, which is both statistically suboptimal (heterogeneous reference group) and may obscure gender-specific effects. Additionally, the heavy-drinking threshold questions in the NIDA screen distinguish only between 'man' and 'woman,' suggesting the study does not accommodate non-binary participants, creating a mismatch with the 'not-male' coding.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: Missing details on YouGov matching/weighting procedures
issues.description: The manuscript states the sample will be 'matched to U.S. representative norms' by YouGov but does not specify which demographic variables will be used for matching, whether survey weights will be provided and used in analyses, or whether the matching procedure introduces any design effects that should be accounted for in power calculations. YouGov uses a propensity-score matching methodology that differs from probability sampling, and OLS regression without appropriate weights may not yield population-representative estimates.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.

issues.subcategory: No pre-specified exclusion criteria
issues.description: Beyond the implicit screening of past-year use for each behavior, no participant exclusion criteria are specified. There is no mention of how to handle participants who may have clinical diagnoses, are in treatment, or have other characteristics that might warrant exclusion or separate analysis. For a registered report, pre-specifying all inclusion/exclusion criteria is essential.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior.

issues.subcategory: Pornography frequency item limited to solo viewing
issues.description: The pornography viewing frequency item in supplemental materials specifies 'Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner),' excluding partnered pornography viewing. This is a narrower operationalization than described in the methods section and inconsistent with the broad definition of pornography provided. This restriction could undercount pornography use frequency, potentially affecting the interaction term.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: Temporal mismatch across measures
issues.description: Different measures use different reference periods: frequency items cover the past 12 months, NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items cover the past 3 months, the BPS covers the last 6 months, and the PGSI covers the last 12 months. These temporal mismatches mean that frequency and problematic use may not correspond to the same time period, potentially attenuating or inflating associations depending on changes in behavior over time.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency ... In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge ... In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you

issues.subcategory: Heterogeneous gambling definition inflates frequency measure
issues.description: The gambling definition includes highly heterogeneous activities ranging from buying lottery tickets (very common, low-risk) to online gambling (less common, higher-risk). A single frequency item averaging across these diverse activities may not be comparable to substance-specific frequency measures. Someone who buys a weekly lottery ticket is counted the same as a weekly online gambler, despite very different risk profiles and moral valence.
issues.quote: gambling refers to any recreational activity in which money or something of value is wagered, bet, or risked for the potential of winning more money. Examples of these types of activities include: gambling in casinos or online, buying lottery tickets, playing fantasy sports for money

issues.subcategory: No attention checks or validity indicators
issues.description: While the authors state that YouGov's proprietary quality controls are sufficient, they do not include any study-specific attention checks, validity indicators, or consistency items. Relying entirely on a vendor's proprietary and opaque quality standards is insufficient for a registered report, as reviewers and readers cannot evaluate the adequacy of those controls.
issues.quote: certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset
